claim: Neural connectomics has begun producing massive amounts of data, necessitating new analysis methods to discover the biological and computational structure.
source: Neural connectomics has begun producing massive amounts of data, necessitating new analysis methods to discover the biological and computational structure.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of the field, drawing from established scientific knowledge about connectomics data generation.

claim: It has long been assumed that discovering neuron types and their relation to microcircuitry is crucial to understanding neural function.
source: It has long been assumed that discovering neuron types and their relation to microcircuitry is crucial to understanding neural function.
evidence: This refers to established scientific consensus in neuroscience.

claim: The authors developed a non-parametric Bayesian technique that identifies neuron types and microcircuitry patterns in connectomics data.
source: Here we developed a non-parametric Bayesian technique that identifies neuron types and microcircuitry patterns in connectomics data.
evidence: This is the primary methodological contribution described in the manuscript.

claim: The technique combines connectivity, cell body location, and the spatial distribution of synapses in a principled and probabilistically coherent manner.
source: It combines the information traditionally used by biologists in a principled and probabilistically coherent manner, including connectivity, cell body location, and the spatial distribution of synapses.
evidence: This describes the features used by the model as presented in the methods.

claim: The approach recovers known neuron types in the retina.
source: We show that the approach recovers known neuron types in the retina and enables predictions of connectivity, better than simpler algorithms.
evidence: This is supported by experimental results shown in the manuscript.

claim: The approach enables predictions of connectivity better than simpler algorithms.
source: We show that the approach recovers known neuron types in the retina and enables predictions of connectivity, better than simpler algorithms.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis with other methods shown in the results.

claim: The approach can reveal interesting structure in the nervous system of Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: It also can reveal interesting structure in the nervous system of Caenorhabditis elegans and an old man-made microprocessor.
evidence: This is demonstrated through application to C. elegans data in the results section.

claim: The approach can reveal interesting structure in an old man-made microprocessor.
source: It also can reveal interesting structure in the nervous system of Caenorhabditis elegans and an old man-made microprocessor.
evidence: This is demonstrated through application to microprocessor data in the results section.

claim: Emerging connectomics techniques promise to quantify the location and connectivity of each neuron within a tissue volume.
source: Emerging connectomics techniques (Zador et al., 2012; Morgan and Lichtman, 2013) promise to quantify the location and connectivity of each neuron within a tissue volume.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in the field.

claim: Massive connectomics datasets will far exceed the capacity of neuroanatomists to manually trace small circuits.
source: These massive datasets will far exceed the capacity of neuroanatomists to manually trace small circuits, thus necessitating computational, quantitative, and automatic methods for understanding neural circuit structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the scale of data being generated.

claim: The rise of sequencing techniques necessitated the development of novel computational methods to understand genomic structure, ushering in bioinformatics as an independent discipline.
source: The impact of this kind of high-throughput transition has been seen before—the rise of sequencing techniques necessitated the development of novel computational methods to understand genomic structure, ushering in bioinformatics as an independent discipline (Koboldt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge about the history of bioinformatics.

claim: The brain consists of multiple kinds of neurons, each of which is hypothesized to have a specific role in overall computation.
source: The brain consists of multiple kinds of neurons, each of which is hypothesized to have a specific role in overall computation.
evidence: This represents established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Neuron types differ in the way they connect to one another.
source: Neuron types differ in many ways, for example, chemical or morphological, but they also differ in the way they connect to one another (Seung and Sümbül, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The idea of well defined, type-dependent local connectivity patterns (microcircuits) has a long history.
source: In fact, the idea of well defined, type-dependent local connectivity patterns (microcircuits) has a long history (Passingham, 2002), and is prominent in many areas, from sensory (e.g., retina; Masland, 2001) to processing (e.g., neocortex; Mountcastle, 1997) to movement (e.g., spinal cord; Grillner et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Types of repeated computing patterns are a common feature of computing systems, even occurring in man-made computing circuits.
source: These types of repeated computing patterns are a common feature of computing systems, even occurring in man-made computing circuits.
evidence: This represents general knowledge about computing systems.

claim: Early network science approaches focused on global graph properties, such as the types of scaling present in the network.
source: Early approaches focused on global graph properties, such as the types of scaling present in the network (Watts and Strogatz, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: More recent network science work aims at identifying very small-scale repeat patterns, or motifs, in networks.
source: While this approach leads to an understanding of the global network, more recent work aims at identifying very small-scale repeat patterns, or motifs, in networks (Milo et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Community-based detection methods and stochastic block models are commonly used algorithms for discovering structure in probabilistic graphs.
source: Commonly used algorithms include community-based detection methods (Girvan and Newman, 2002) and stochastic block models (Nowicki and Snijders, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Traditional graph clustering approaches can incorporate the probabilistic nature of neural connections.
source: While these approaches can incorporate the probabilistic nature of neural connections (Hill et al., 2012), they do not incorporate the additional richer structure present in connectomics data—the location of cell bodies, the spatial distribution of synapses, and the distances between neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Traditional graph clustering approaches do not incorporate the location of cell bodies, the spatial distribution of synapses, and the distances between neurons.
source: While these approaches can incorporate the probabilistic nature of neural connections (Hill et al., 2012), they do not incorporate the additional richer structure present in connectomics data—the location of cell bodies, the spatial distribution of synapses, and the distances between neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of existing methods.

claim: The probability of connections has a strong spatial component in neural systems.
source: It is of particular importance that the probability of connections has a strong spatial component, a factor that is hard to reconcile with many other methods.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about neural connectivity.

claim: Patterns of connectivity in neuroscience and other computing systems are expected to be much more complex than traditional motifs, exhibiting a strong spatial dependence.
source: When it comes to neuroscience and other computing systems, we expect patterns of connectivity much more complex than traditional motifs, exhibiting a strong spatial dependence arising from the complex genetic, chemical, and activity-based neural development processes.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of neural development processes.

claim: The Bayesian non-parametric model can discover circuit structure automatically from connectomics data: the cell types, their spatial patterns of interconnection, and the locations of somata and synapses.
source: To address these challenges, here we describe a Bayesian non-parametric model that can discover circuit structure automatically from connectomics data: the cell types, their spatial patterns of interconnection, and the locations of somata and synapses.
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the model as demonstrated in the results.

claim: By incorporating additional information, the model both accurately predicts the connection as well as agrees with human neuroanatomists as to the identification of cell types.
source: We show that by incorporating this additional information, our model both accurately predicts the connection as well as agrees with human neuroanatomists as to the identification of cell types.
evidence: This is supported by experimental results comparing the model to human annotations.

claim: The authors take inspiration from previous work on identifying cell types automatically from morphology.
source: We take as inspiration previous work on identifying cell types automatically from morphology (Guerra et al., 2011) and electrophysiology (Druckmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The authors take inspiration from previous work on identifying cell types automatically from electrophysiology.
source: We take as inspiration previous work on identifying cell types automatically from morphology (Guerra et al., 2011) and electrophysiology (Druckmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The authors primarily focus on the recently released mouse retina connectome.
source: We primarily focus on the recently released mouse retina connectome (Helmstaedter et al., 2013), but additionally examine the Caenorhabditis elegans connectome (White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citation and describes the datasets used.

claim: The authors additionally examine the Caenorhabditis elegans connectome.
source: We primarily focus on the recently released mouse retina connectome (Helmstaedter et al., 2013), but additionally examine the Caenorhabditis elegans connectome (White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citation and describes the datasets used.

claim: Comparing the cell types discovered by the algorithms with those obtained manually by human anatomists reveals a high degree of agreement.
source: Comparing the cell types discovered by the algorithms with those obtained manually by human anatomists reveals a high degree of agreement.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative comparison metrics shown in the results.

claim: The model begins with the generic notion of a cell being a member of a single type.
source: We build a structured probabilistic model which begins with the generic notion of a cell being a member of a single type—and these types affect soma depth, distribution of synapses, as well as a cell type and distance-dependent connection probability.
evidence: This describes the assumptions of the model.

claim: Cell types affect soma depth, distribution of synapses, as well as a cell type and distance-dependent connection probability.
source: We build a structured probabilistic model which begins with the generic notion of a cell being a member of a single type—and these types affect soma depth, distribution of synapses, as well as a cell type and distance-dependent connection probability.
evidence: This describes the assumptions of the model.

claim: The method is unsupervised—it seeks to discover structure in data and make predictions in the absence of training data.
source: In machine learning parlance, our method is unsupervised—it seeks to discover structure in data and make predictions in the absence of training data.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach.

claim: The model takes as input the connectivity matrix of cells, a matrix of the distance between cells, the per-cell soma depth, and the depth profile of the cell's synapses.
source: We take as input (Figure 1A) the connectivity matrix of cells (Figure 1B), a matrix of the distance between cells (Figure 1C), the per-cell soma depth (Figure 1D), and the depth profile of the cell's synapses (Figure 1E).
evidence: This describes the input data to the model and references Figure 1.

claim: The model performs joint probabilistic inference to automatically learn the number of cell types, which cells belong to which type, their type-specific connectivity, and how connections between types vary with distance.
source: We perform joint probabilistic inference to automatically learn the number of cell types, which cells belong to which type, their type-specific connectivity, and how connections between types vary with distance.
evidence: This describes the outputs of the model inference.

claim: The model simultaneously learns the soma depth associated with each type and the typical synaptic density profile.
source: We also simultaneously learn the soma depth associated with each type and the typical synaptic density profile (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This describes additional outputs of the model and references Figure 1.

claim: The model starts with the iSBM, which has been shown to meaningfully cluster connection graphs while learning the number of hidden groups.
source: We start with a model for connectivity, the iSBM (Kemp et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2006), which has been shown to meaningfully cluster connection graphs while learning the number of hidden groups, or types.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on the iSBM.

claim: The authors extend the iSBM approach by adding distance dependence to model salient aspects of microcircuitry via logistic and exponential distance-link functions.
source: We extend this approach by adding distance dependence to model salient aspects of microcircuitry via logistic and exponential distance-link functions.
evidence: This describes the methodological contribution of the paper.

claim: The model forms a unimodal model of cell body depth and a multimodal synapse density profile model.
source: We form a unimodial model of cell body depth and a multimodal synapse density profile model (see 'Materials and methods' for mathematical details).
evidence: This describes components of the model.

claim: If the model works well, then the probability that a pair of neurons is of the same type should be high if the neurons actually are of the same type.
source: First, if the model works well, then the probability that a pair of neurons is of the same type should be high if the neurons actually are of the same type.
evidence: This describes an evaluation criterion for the model.

claim: The model should assign a high probability of connection between two cells if they have a connection in the underlying data.
source: Second, the model should assign a high probability of connection between two cells if they have a connection in the underlying data.
evidence: This describes an evaluation criterion for the model.

claim: Homogeneity reflects the degree to which a found cluster or type contains only a single true type.
source: Homogeneity reflects the degree to which a found cluster or type contains only a single true type.
evidence: This defines a metric used in the evaluation.

claim: Completeness measures how much of a true type is contained within a single identified type.
source: Completeness measures how much of a true type is contained within a single identified type—a completeness of 1.0 means no true type is split into multiple subtypes.
evidence: This defines a metric used in the evaluation.

claim: ARI is a metric that reflects both homogeneity and completeness measures.
source: ARI is a metric that reflects both measures (see the supplemental material for more information).
evidence: This defines a metric used in the evaluation.

claim: The model does a good job of recovering the correct number of cell types in simulated data.
source: We find that the model does a good job of recovering the correct number of cell types (Figure 2A), the cell identities (Figure 2B), and the spatial extent of each type (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by results from simulated data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The model does a good job of recovering cell identities in simulated data.
source: We find that the model does a good job of recovering the correct number of cell types (Figure 2A), the cell identities (Figure 2B), and the spatial extent of each type (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by results from simulated data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The model does a good job of recovering the spatial extent of each type in simulated data.
source: We find that the model does a good job of recovering the correct number of cell types (Figure 2A), the cell identities (Figure 2B), and the spatial extent of each type (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by results from simulated data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The regular block model (iSBM) cannot correctly deal with distance-dependent connectivity.
source: This contrast shows that while the regular block model can not correctly deal with distance-dependent connectivity, our model can.
evidence: This is supported by comparative results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The authors' model can correctly deal with distance-dependent connectivity.
source: This contrast shows that while the regular block model can not correctly deal with distance-dependent connectivity, our model can.
evidence: This is supported by comparative results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The model converges relatively quickly to an estimate of the most probable values for the cell types.
source: Our model converges relatively quickly (see 'Mixing of Markov chains') to an estimate of the most probable values for the cell types, which is enabled by using a combination of simulated annealing and parallelized Markov-chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) (see 'Materials and methods' for details).
evidence: This is supported by convergence analysis shown in the methods section.

claim: If the data are sampled from the authors' model, inference according to their model is good by all measures.
source: If the data are sampled from our model, inference according to our model, unsurprisingly, is good by all measures.
evidence: This is supported by results shown in Figure 3.

claim: If the data come from a block model without distance dependence, the model still does well on all meaningful measures.
source: If the data come from a block model without distance dependence, we see that it still does well on all meaningful measures (Figure 3, second row).
evidence: This is supported by results shown in Figure 3.

claim: For the mixed membership model, the model grossly overestimates the number of types, by basically allocating a type for each combination of memberships.
source: For the mixed membership model (Figure 3, third row), the model grossly overestimates the number of types, by basically allocating a type for each combination of memberships.
evidence: This is supported by results shown in Figure 3.

claim: For the latent position clustering model, the model does poorly.
source: Lastly, for the latent position clustering model (Figure 3, fourth row), the model does poorly.
evidence: This is supported by results shown in Figure 3.

claim: If type is continuous instead of discrete, then the model is basically trying to cover a continuous set with a discrete scenario leading to rather poor performance.
source: If type is continuous instead of discrete, then our model is basically trying to cover a continuous set with a discrete scenario leading to rather poor performance.
evidence: This is an inference about model limitations based on the results.

claim: Cell types are expected to have a discrete biological basis.
source: However, as we do expect cell types to have a discrete biological basis, we might expect our model to do well with real data.
evidence: This represents established biological knowledge.

claim: If there is no distance dependence, edge effects do not artificially introduce distance dependence.
source: We find that, if there is no distance dependence, edge effects do not artificially introduce distance dependence.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4.

claim: If the section being examined is too small, the model can miss the distance dependence.
source: However, if the section we are examining is too small, our model can miss the distance dependence.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4.

claim: With respect to distance-dependent connectivity inference, the model errs on the side of caution.
source: Thus with respect to distance-dependent connectivity inference, our model errs on the side of caution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the edge effect analysis.

claim: For spatial extent that is similar to the currently available datasets, the effects of edge artifacts are quite limited.
source: But we also find that for spatial extent that is similar to the currently available datasets, the effects of this are quite limited.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The mouse retina is a neural circuit which is expected to have connectivity patterns that are well approximated by the generative model.
source: The mouse retina (Masland, 2001) is a neural circuit which we expect to have connectivity patterns that are well approximated by our generative model.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of retinal structure and is supported by citation.

claim: There are multiple classes of cells in the retina that can be broadly grouped into: ganglion cells that transmit information to the rest of the brain; bipolar cells that connect between different cells; and amacrine cells that feed into the ganglion cells.
source: It is known that there are multiple classes of cells that can be broadly grouped into: ganglion cells that transmit information to the rest of the brain; bipolar cells that connect between different cells; and amacrine cells that feed into the ganglion cells.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about retinal cell types.

claim: Recent research has produced a large dataset containing both the types of cells from orthogonal approaches, and also the connectivity matrix between all reconstructed cells.
source: Recent research (Helmstaedter et al., 2013) has produced a large dataset containing both the types of cells from orthogonal approaches, and also the connectivity matrix between all reconstructed cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the dataset source.

claim: The algorithm took 8 hr to perform inference on the retina data.
source: The algorithm took 8 hr to perform inference, dividing neurons into a set of cell types which reflect known neuroanatomical distinctions (Figure 5 shows the MAP result).
evidence: This is a direct measurement of computational performance.

claim: The algorithm divides neurons into a set of cell types which reflect known neuroanatomical distinctions.
source: The algorithm took 8 hr to perform inference, dividing neurons into a set of cell types which reflect known neuroanatomical distinctions (Figure 5 shows the MAP result).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 5.

claim: For each pair of neurons there is a specific distance-dependent connection probability, which is well approximated by the model fit.
source: For each pair of neurons there is a specific distance-dependent connection probability (Figure 5D), which is well approximated by the model fit.
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Each type of cell is rather isotropically distributed across space.
source: Moreover, each type of cell is rather isotropically distributed across space (Figure 5C) as should be expected for true cell types.
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The discovered types closely reflect the (anatomist-determined) segmentation of cells into retinal ganglion, narrow amacrine, medium/wide amacrine, and bipolar cells.
source: Our types closely reflect the (anatomist-determined) segmentation of cells into retinal ganglion, narrow amacrine, medium/wide amacrine, and bipolar cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The discovered types tend to reflect the known laminar distribution in the retina.
source: We find that the types we find tend to reflect the known laminar distribution in the retina (Figure 6C) as well as the known synaptic density profiles.
evidence: This is supported by results shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The discovered types tend to reflect the known synaptic density profiles.
source: We find that the types we find tend to reflect the known laminar distribution in the retina (Figure 6C) as well as the known synaptic density profiles.
evidence: This is supported by results shown in the manuscript.

claim: The algorithm yields a separation of neurons into a smaller number of types than the fully granular listing of 71 types found by the original authors of the paper.
source: The algorithm yields a separation of neurons into a smaller number of types than the fully granular listing of 71 types found by the original authors of the paper (Helmstaedter et al., 2013), although it is still highly correlated with those finer type distinctions (see section 'Mouse retina').
evidence: This is supported by comparison with the original dataset annotations.

claim: The algorithm's clustering is still highly correlated with the finer type distinctions found by the original authors.
source: The algorithm yields a separation of neurons into a smaller number of types than the fully granular listing of 71 types found by the original authors of the paper (Helmstaedter et al., 2013), although it is still highly correlated with those finer type distinctions (see section 'Mouse retina').
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis mentioned in the text.

claim: With larger datasets, even closer agreement with anatomist classifications would be found.
source: It is our expectation that, with larger datasets, even closer agreement would be found.
evidence: This is a speculation about future performance with more data.

claim: The model tends to over-cluster—cells which are of distinct type (at the finest granularity of neuroanatomist-identified type) are grouped as a single type by the model.
source: We see that our model tends to over-cluster—cells which are of distinct type (at the finest granularity of neuroanatomist-identified type) are grouped as a single type by our model.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the clustering results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Many techniques allow for good link-predictive accuracy on the retina dataset.
source: We find that given the dataset, many techniques allow for good link-predictive accuracy.
evidence: This is supported by comparative results shown in Figure 6G.

claim: All the methods allow decent link prediction with an AUC in the 0.9 range.
source: All the methods allow decent link prediction with an AUC in the 0.9 range.
evidence: This is supported by results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The authors' algorithm clearly outperforms the simple statistical models that only use connectivity for link prediction.
source: However, our algorithm clearly outperforms the simple statistical models that only use connectivity.
evidence: This is supported by comparative results shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The authors' algorithm far outperforms the controls in terms of clustering accuracy (ARI).
source: We find that our algorithm far outperforms the controls.
evidence: This is supported by comparative results shown in Figure 6G.

claim: When the model is based on more of the same information used by anatomists, then it gets better at agreeing with these anatomists.
source: We also find that when it is based on more of the same information used by anatomists, then it gets better at agreeing with these anatomists.
evidence: This is supported by comparative results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Using connectivity, distance, synapse distribution, and soma depth leads to the highest ARI.
source: In particular, using connectivity, distance, synapse distribution, and soma depth leads to the highest ARI.
evidence: This is supported by comparative results shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the absence of distance information, mere connectivity information results in types which only span a small region of space—essentially local cliques.
source: We see that, in the absence of distance information, mere connectivity information results in types which only span a small region of space—essentially local cliques.
evidence: This is supported by results shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Incorporation of distance information results in types which span the entire extent of the layer.
source: Incorporation of distance information results in types which span the entire extent of the layer.
evidence: This is supported by results shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The depth variance of all models continues to be substantially larger than that predicted by human anatomists.
source: The depth variance of all models continues to be substantially larger than that predicted by human anatomists—future directions of work include attempting to more strongly encode this prior belief of laminarity.
evidence: This is supported by results shown in Figure 6H.

claim: C. elegans is a model system in developmental neuroscience, with the location and connectivity of each of 302 neurons developmentally determined, leading to early measurement of the connectome.
source: C. elegans is a model system in developmental neuroscience (White et al., 1986), with the location and connectivity of each of 302 neurons developmentally determined, leading to early measurement of the connectome.
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: Unlike the retina, only the motor neurons in C. elegans exhibit regular distribution in space—along the body axis.
source: Unlike the retina, only the motor neurons in C. elegans exhibit regular distribution in space—along the body axis.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about C. elegans anatomy.

claim: Most interneurons in C. elegans are concentrated in various ganglia that project throughout the entire animal.
source: Most interneurons are concentrated in various ganglia that project throughout the entire animal, and the sensory neurons are primarily located in a small number of anterior ganglia.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about C. elegans anatomy.

claim: The sensory neurons in C. elegans are primarily located in a small number of anterior ganglia.
source: Most interneurons are concentrated in various ganglia that project throughout the entire animal, and the sensory neurons are primarily located in a small number of anterior ganglia.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about C. elegans anatomy.

claim: The measured C. elegans connectome is actually two separate graphs—one of directed chemical synapses and another of undirected electrical synapses.
source: C. elegans also differs from the retina in that the measured connectome is actually two separate graphs—one of directed chemical synapses and another of undirected electrical synapses.
evidence: This describes the structure of the C. elegans dataset.

claim: A superficial inspection of the C. elegans results shows clustering into groups consisting roughly homogeneously of motor neurons, sensory neurons, and interneurons.
source: A superficial inspection of the results shows clustering into groups consisting roughly homogeneously of motor neurons, sensory neurons, and interneurons.
evidence: This is supported by results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Closer examination of C. elegans results reveals agreement with the classifications originally outlined by White in 1986.
source: Closer examination reveals agreement with the classifications originally outlined by White in 1986 (White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with the original classifications and citation.

claim: The clustering of C. elegans neurons does not perfectly reflect known divisions.
source: Note our clustering does not perfectly reflect known divisions—several combinations of head and sensory neurons are combined, and a difficult-to-explain group of mostly VB and DB motor neuron types, with VC split between various groups.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The identified C. elegans cell types reflect a 'coarsening' of known types, based entirely on connectivity and distance information.
source: Our identified cell types thus reflect a 'coarsening' of known types, based entirely on connectivity and distance information, even when the organism exhibits substantially less spatial regularity than the retina.
evidence: This is an inference based on the results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Computer architects use common patterns of transistors when designing circuits, with each transistor having a 'type' in the circuit.
source: Computer architects use common patterns of transistors when designing circuits, with each transistor having a 'type' in the circuit.
evidence: This represents general knowledge about computer architecture.

claim: The algorithm identifies areas of spatial homogeneity in the microprocessor that mirror the known structure in the underlying architecture of the circuit.
source: Our algorithm identifies areas of spatial homogeneity that mirror the known structure in the underlying architecture of the circuit, segmenting transistor types recognizable to computer architects.
evidence: This is supported by results shown in Figure 8.

claim: One identified type in the microprocessor contains the 'clocked' transistors, which retain digital state.
source: Using the original schematics, we see that one identified type contains the 'clocked' transistors, which retain digital state.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with the original schematics and results shown in Figure 8.

claim: Two identified types in the microprocessor contain transistors with pins C1 or C2 connected to ground, mostly serving as inverters.
source: Two other types contain transistors with pins C1 or C2 connected to ground, mostly serving as inverters.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with the original schematics and results shown in Figure 8.

claim: An additional identified type in the microprocessor controls the behavior of the three registers of interest (X, Y, and S) with respect to the SB data bus.
source: An additional identified type controls the behavior of the three registers of interest (X, Y, and S) with respect to the SB data bus, either allowing them to latch or drive data from the bus.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with the original schematics and results shown in Figure 8.

claim: The repeat patterns of spatial connectivity are visible in the microprocessor, showing the man-made horizontal and vertical layout of the same types of transistors.
source: The repeat patterns of spatial connectivity are visible in Figure 8C, showing the man-made horizontal and vertical layout of the same types of transistors.
evidence: This is supported by results shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The incorporation of all available data types yields results that combine both high link-prediction accuracy and high agreement with human anatomists.
source: When compared to existing methods, we show how the incorporation of all of this data yields results that combine both high link-prediction accuracy and high agreement with human anatomists.
evidence: This is supported by comparative results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Combining the available data types allows discovery of cell types and microcircuitry that were known to exist in the systems based on decades of previous research.
source: We have found that combining the available data types allows us to discover cell types and microcircuitry that were known to exist in the systems based on decades of previous research and allows good prediction of connectivity.
evidence: This is supported by results across all three datasets.

claim: No known solution exists to exactly find the most probable parsing of the neurons into cell types and connectivity patterns for the probabilistic models used.
source: For our probabilistic models, no known solution exists to exactly find the most probable parsing of the neurons into cell types and connectivity patterns.
evidence: This represents knowledge about the computational complexity of the problem.

claim: While different initializations converge to similar ultimate values, the global optimum can never realistically be obtained.
source: We employ a collection of MCMC techniques (see 'Materials and methods'), but while different initializations converge to similar ultimate values, we can never realistically obtain the global optimum.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of the MCMC approach.

claim: For the probabilistic model, inference becomes slower as the amount of data increases.
source: For our probabilistic model, inference becomes slower as the amount of data increases.
evidence: This is a general property of the computational approach.

claim: The algorithm required several hours for 1000 neurons.
source: Our algorithm required several hours for 1000 neurons.
evidence: This is a direct measurement of computational performance.

claim: Larger datasets will allow algorithms to distinguish more distinct types.
source: Larger datasets will allow algorithms to distinguish more distinct types and we expect closer agreement with existing anatomical knowledge as more data become available.
evidence: This is a speculation about future performance with more data.

claim: Closer agreement with existing anatomical knowledge is expected as more data become available.
source: Larger datasets will allow algorithms to distinguish more distinct types and we expect closer agreement with existing anatomical knowledge as more data become available.
evidence: This is a speculation about future performance with more data.

claim: In general, for such problems precision increases with the size of the dataset.
source: Moreover, in general, for such problems precision increases with the size of the dataset and the cells that we have are not sufficient to statistically distinguish all the cell types known in anatomy (such as the ∼70 in the retina).
evidence: This represents general knowledge about statistical inference.

claim: The cells available in the dataset are not sufficient to statistically distinguish all the cell types known in anatomy (such as the ∼70 in the retina).
